To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Prdm12 is a key determinant of V1 interneuronal specification in vertebrates, but not in amphioxus.
the specification of V1 interneuronal progenitors in vertebrates requires Prdm12.

1) Prdm12 is expressed in the p1 domain of the hindbrain/spinal cord, 2) Prdm12 expression is dependent on Pax6 and RA and is restricted to p2 progenitors by Dbx1/Nkx6, 3) Prdm12 acts as a general determinant for V1 interneuronal fate by repressing DbX1 and NkX6.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how the vertebrate nervous system forms.
the development of the central nervous system, and in particular, with the specification of the V1 interneuronal population.
the molecular mechanisms that control the genesis of inhibitory neurons in vertebrate embryos, with a special emphasis on the V1 neurons.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Prdm12 is a transcription factor required for the specification and differentiation of V1 interneurones.
V1 interneurogenesis is dependent on the transcription factor PrDM12.
the Prdm12 gene is a general determinant of the V1 cell fate in the caudalmost neural tube, at least in the frog embryo.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
V1 interneuronal specification requires Prdm2, whose expression is restricted to the P1 domain by cross-repressive interactions of Dbx1/Nkx6 and Prdm2.
Prdm12 is a determinant of V1 fate, and that this function is achieved through a cross-repressive mechanism involving Dbx1 and the vertebrate Nkx6 homologues.
Prdm12 is a general determinant of the V1 interneuronal identity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Prdm12 specifies V-1 interneurons by repressing Dbf1 and Nk6-1/6-2.
Prdm12 is a general determinant of the fate of V1 interneuronal cells.

Prdm12 is an essential determinant of V1 cells, at least in frogs, and that its expression is controlled by a cross-repressive network involving Dbx1 and the Nkx6 proteins, which is probably conserved in other vertebrates.
